parts.note: reads like a request for a sip, but describes the most famous waterfall drop of North America

explanation.surface: Someone politely asks for a little water to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A drop of water' sounds like a small sip, but here it is a huge fall of water, the falls on the US-Canada border.
explanation.definitionFit: The great falls on the US-Canada border are a vast plunge of a river over a cliff.

clue.text: Until Pa changes, this ceremony can't take place !

definitions.text: Until Pa changes, this ceremony can't take place !

indicators.note: the letters of the two words before are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A wedding is held up until the father changes his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges UNTIL PA; read whole, the clue says a wedding waits for Father's consent.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a wedding, the marriage ceremony that cannot go ahead without the father's blessing.

clue.text: The lion's share rejected in gratitude ?

definitions.text: The lion's share rejected in gratitude ?

parts.words: The lion's share rejected in gratitude ?
parts.note: recalls the fable of the slave whom a lion refused to eat because he had once pulled a thorn from its paw

explanation.surface: A lion turns down its biggest portion out of thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The lion's share' looks like the largest part, but here it is the lion's meal: in the fable the lion spares the man who took a thorn from its paw.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman tale this escaped slave was spared in the arena by the lion he had once helped.

parts.note: Naaman in 2 Kings asks whether the rivers of Damascus are not better than all the waters of Israel

explanation.surface: A plain description of a Syrian river.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2 Kings 5:12 Naaman names 'Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus'.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical name for the Barada, the stream that waters Damascus.

parts.note: a triton is also a newt, not the sea god Wordsworth hoped to hear blow his horn

explanation.surface: A reference to the sea god in Wordsworth's sonnet, disowned.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's 'The World Is Too Much with Us' wishes to 'hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn'; the other triton is a newt, which lives both in water and on land.
explanation.definitionFit: A newt is a cold-blooded creature that lives both in water and on land.

parts.note: names an old variety of apple that the street sellers of fruit took their trade name from

explanation.surface: A question about what fruit the first street trader sold.
explanation.walkthrough: A costermonger (a London street seller with a barrow) was first a 'costard-monger', a seller of this large old English apple.
explanation.definitionFit: This large ribbed cooking apple gave its name to the costermonger, the original fruit-seller with a barrow.

clue.text: Stop taking care of half our capital

parts.note: c/o is the postal abbreviation for care of

indicators.note: only one of the two halves of the city's name is kept

parts.note: London is the British capital

explanation.surface: A halt is called to looking after part of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps LON of LONDON. 'Stop' is the punctuation mark, not a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark of two dots is a stop, a mark that pauses the reader.

clue.text: Wine in splendid condition for a football fan

indicators.note: the wine is placed inside the word for splendid

parts.note: super means splendid
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Wine served in top condition to a football follower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'condition' belongs with 'splendid': 'in splendid condition' reads as healthy, but it gives the word for splendid, with the wine set inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan backs a team, so is one of its followers.

clue.text: Got up in a shade of pink

definitions.meaning: rose from bed or a seat

explanation.surface: Someone dressed up in pink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got up' can also mean dressed, which fits 'in a shade of pink', but it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of rise means stood or climbed out of bed, and split as two words it is a pinkish hue.

parts.note: looks like a star of the French stage, but means the senior woman of a group, a word borrowed from French

explanation.surface: A question about a star actress of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading lady' suggests an actress, but it is the most senior woman in a field, a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior and most respected woman in a profession is the female dean of the group.

parts.note: a quotation from the opening scene of The Taming of the Shrew, where Lucentio praises the Italian university city

explanation.surface: A quotation with its source, The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 Scene 1 Lucentio says he has come to 'fair Padua, nursery of arts'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Lucentio calls this north Italian university town the nursery of arts, a place where learning grows.

parts.note: describes the style of music a madrigal is written in, several independent voice parts sung together

explanation.surface: A heading naming the kind of music found in madrigals.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrigals are part-songs in which several independent melodic lines are sung at once, the many-voiced texture.

clue.text: Life on Innisfree can be splendid

definitions.text: Life on Innisfree can be splendid

parts.words: Life on Innisfree can be splendid
parts.note: Yeats wished to live alone on the lake island of Innisfree, and the phrase 'splendid ...' is a set expression for aloofness

explanation.surface: A remark that living on Yeats's lake island would be wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'The Lake Isle of Innisfree' Yeats longs to 'live alone in the bee-loud glade'; Britain's nineteenth-century aloofness from alliances was called 'splendid isolation'.
explanation.definitionFit: Living alone on a remote island is a state of solitude, cut off from others.

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
on means about, as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: A poem written about the theatre of ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek odeion was a small roofed theatre for music and recitals.

parts.note: a berceuse is a cradle song, so a specialist in them would write lullabies, which suggests the name of a French baroque composer

explanation.surface: A question about which composer was a specialist in cradle songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Berceuses are lullabies; Jean-Baptiste Lully, court composer to Louis XIV, has a name that sounds like 'lullaby'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Baptiste Lully was the leading composer at the court of Louis XIV.

clue.text: It's famous for more than one sort of batter

definitions.text: It's famous for more than one sort of batter

parts.words: It's famous for more than one sort of batter
parts.note: a northern English county known both for its pudding batter and its cricket batsmen

explanation.surface: Something is known for several kinds of cooking batter.
explanation.walkthrough: The county gives its name to Yorkshire pudding, made from batter, and has produced many great cricket batsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: The English county is known for its baked batter pudding and for its cricketing batters.

clue.text: Once tempi are changed, there is loss of power

indicators.note: the letters of the two words before are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A musician finds that after the tempos shift, the music loses its force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are changed' rearranges ONCE TEMPI.
explanation.definitionFit: Impotence is weakness, a lack of strength or ability to act.

parts.note: country folk said with an h sound added become game birds that fly up when flushed

explanation.surface: Ambitious country people who breathe heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: Add an aspirate, the H sound, to PEASANTS (rustics) and you get game birds that rise high when flushed.
explanation.definitionFit: Game birds shot as they fly up are these rustics with an added h.

clue.text: William and Mary not quite their favoured style !

definitions.text: William and Mary not quite their favoured style !

parts.words: William and Mary not quite their favoured style !
parts.note: clergy who refused the oath of allegiance to the new monarchs in 1689 did not favour them, as if they disliked the furniture style

explanation.surface: Some people did not care for William and Mary furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'William and Mary' is also a style of furniture, but here they are the monarchs: clergy who refused to swear allegiance to them in 1689 were these.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy who would not swear the oath to William and Mary were people refusing that oath.

clue.text: Plenty of brass from the underwriter ?

definitions.meaning: brass is slang for cheek, so plenty of it is self-confidence
an underwriter provides cover against loss, the British word for insurance on a life

explanation.surface: Lots of money comes from the insurer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like money, which suits the underwriter, but here it is nerve; in Britain life cover is often called this rather than insurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-confidence is boldness or nerve, and the same word is the British term for life insurance cover.

clue.text: Takes a couple of hundred unruly pets

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two of them make CC

indicators.note: out of control, so the letters of the next word are disordered

explanation.surface: Someone takes on two hundred badly behaved animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unruly' rearranges PETS to EPTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Receives or agrees to, as in taking a gift or an offer.

parts.note: a gap to fill in a line from Poe's poem The Bells, describing the old Norse letter style

explanation.surface: A line from Poe with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Poe's 'The Bells' has 'Keeping time, time, time, / In a sort of Runic rhyme'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes the old Germanic alphabet's letters, and so something ancient and mysterious.

clue.text: He takes the field with a good seat

definitions.text: He takes the field with a good seat

parts.words: He takes the field with a good seat
parts.note: adding the word field gives the name of a deep leather sofa

explanation.surface: A horseman rides out to the field sitting well in the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: Add 'field' and you have a chesterfield, a padded sofa, a good seat; the surface suggests a rider.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined to the word field it makes a buttoned leather sofa, a comfortable seat.

definitions.meaning: to cast a column of figures is to total it
throws, as of dice or a fishing line

explanation.surface: Someone totals the scores from the throws.
explanation.definitionFit: Totalling figures is an old sense of the verb, and throws of dice or line are nouns of the same word.

parts.note: an artist's model undresses, and a cartoonist draws a line of panels

explanation.surface: A question about what a cartoonist's model does.
explanation.walkthrough: An artist's model undresses (strips), and a cartoonist draws a comic strip.
explanation.definitionFit: Undresses, as a life model does, and also a row of cartoon panels.

definitions.meaning: an organisation such as a college or society

explanation.surface: Someone founds an organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to found or start; as a noun, an organisation devoted to a cause.

parts.note: looks like a story set in France's capital, but means a poem about the Trojan prince who took Helen

explanation.surface: A grand story set in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parisian' suggests the French city, but it is Paris the Trojan prince, whose abduction of Helen began the war Homer tells of.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's poem of the Trojan War, started when Paris carried off Helen.

definitions.meaning: a single edition of a paper

explanation.surface: A paper written for children.
explanation.definitionFit: Offspring are a person's descendants, and one printing of a paper is a single edition.

clue.text: " To" bottomless-, there to dwell In adamantine chains (Milton)

definitions.text: " To" bottomless-, there to dwell In adamantine chains (Milton)

parts.words: " To" bottomless-, there to dwell In adamantine chains (Milton)
parts.note: a gap to fill in Paradise Lost, Book 1, where Satan is hurled into eternal ruin

explanation.surface: A line from Milton's Paradise Lost with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Paradise Lost, Book 1: Satan is hurled 'To bottomless perdition, there to dwell / In adamantine chains and penal fire'.
explanation.definitionFit: Damnation, the eternal ruin of a soul in hell, is what Satan is cast into.

definitions.meaning: a nose, as in the nickname for someone with a big nose
The tinker in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a nosy travelling mender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosey' reads as inquisitive, but it is a nickname for a big nose; Shakespeare's tinker in A Midsummer Night's Dream plays the Wall.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's nose is called this, and it is also the name of Shakespeare's tinker in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Simpleton at the end of the trench ?

definitions.text: at the end of the trench
definitions.meaning: a sap is a military trench dug towards the enemy, and its forward end is its head

explanation.surface: A fool stands at the far end of a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: In siege warfare a sap is a trench pushed towards enemy lines; its leading end is the sap-head.
explanation.definitionFit: A foolish person is a sap, and the forward point of a siege trench is the sap's head.

clue.text: " I called him Brother, Englishman and Friend !", said Wordsworth

definitions.text: " I called him Brother, Englishman and Friend !", said Wordsworth

parts.words: " I called him Brother, Englishman and Friend !", said Wordsworth
parts.note: a line from The Prelude, Book 3, about the Elizabethan poet Wordsworth admired

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth about a fellow poet.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Prelude Book 3, Wordsworth writes of 'Sweet Spenser' that 'I called him Brother, Englishman, and Friend!'
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser, author of The Faerie Queene, is the Elizabethan poet Wordsworth addresses in The Prelude.
